Minling Chen, Yue Zhang and Jing Xue

School of Economics and Management, Xi’an Shiyou University, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China

Taking into account the characteristics of human-AI interaction, this study seeks to answer the question of the non-linear impact of human-AI interaction on employee creativity. Utilising 284 **KEYWORDS**Human-AI interaction; data from China’s smart manufacturing industry, the results show that the impact of human-AI cognitive outsourcing; interaction on employee creativity is nonlinear, showing an increasing and then decreasing employee creativity; trend. Second, cognitive outsourcing plays a curve mediating role between the two, which is nonlinear eﬀects manifested in the fact that human-AI interaction a ects creativity by inducing an inverted U- shaped change in cognitive outsourcing and then a ecting creativity. Finally, team mastery 

motivational climate moderated the inverted U-shaped relationship between human-AI interaction and cognitive outsourcing. This study practically helps companies to develop 

appropriate human-AI interaction strategies to enhance the core competitiveness of organisations in the smart era.

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into human innovation tasks, its role has evolved from pas- sive assistance to active collaboration, necessitating a deeper exploration of the intrinsic pathways through which AI in uences employee creativity. Cognitive out- sourcing is grounded in distributed cognition (Liu, Ner- sessian, and Stasko 2008). When external information entropy exceeds a certain threshold, humans achieve synergy between internal and external cognitive net- works by ‘outsourcing’ speciﬁc cognitive tasks – such as information retrieval and memory substitution – to external intelligent devices. In the context of AI appli- cations, cognitive o oading is often confused with cog- nitive outsourcing. Cognitive o oading constitutes an instinctive response driven by cognitive load, whose core mechanism lies in leveraging external resources to optimise the brain’s ﬁnite processing capacity while retaining cognitive control within the individual.

The nonlinear e ect of HAI on employee creativity and its mechanism of action are empirically examined using employees of Chinese smart manufacturing companies as the research object. In this study, contributions are made in the following aspects: ﬁrst, compared with the positive e ects of augmented HAI or the negative e ects of automated AI, this paper uniquely proposes the nonlinear e ects of HAI on creativity. It conﬁrms that HAI does not have a simple linear e ect on individ- ual creativity, providing a new theoretical perspective for studying the relationship between HAI and 

employee creativity. Second, based on the resource con- servation theory, the internal mechanism of HAI a ect- ing employee creativity is analyzed. The mediating role of cognitive outsourcing opens the ‘black box’ of human-AI interaction on creativity and exposes the knowledge paradox of AI application. Third, we empha- sise the in uence of organisational factors on employee creativity in HAI, enriching the research literature on the motivational climate of team mastery.

# 2. Theoretical analysis and research hypotheses

## _2.1. The inverted U-shape of human-AI interaction on employee creativity_

The COR theory is an important motivational theory that centres on explaining how individuals protect and acquire valuable resources (Halbesleben et al. 2014). HAI empowers the sustainable development of employ- ees’ creativity in the following ways: ﬁrst, employees enhance their knowledge integration ability with the help of HAI, which is a process of e ective use and reuse of knowledge resources (Zahra, Neubaum, and Hayton [2020)](#5465annals20170093-my-daily-tasks-relies-more-on-ai-zhang-q-x-h-wang-c-g-nerstad-h-ren-and-r-gao-co8-the-more-i-rely-on-ai-the-more-i-feel-that-my-ability-to-think-2022-motivational-climates-work-passion-and-independently-is-diminishing). When employees achieve e ective accumulation of knowledge resources due to AI assist- ance, it then lays the resource foundation for the stimu- lation of creativity and innovative behaviour. Knowledge integration promotes organisational inno- vation (Chen et al. 2021; Tsou 2012), and the ability to use existing knowledge and information to generate di erent combinations and reconﬁgurations is a source of innovation. Second, moderate HAI takes employees away from tedious tasks (Vrontis et al. 2022) and focuses their attention on creative tasks. And due to the change in interaction objects, employees are motiv- ated to move from traditional learning methods to more technology-driven learning approaches (Markauskaite et al. 2022), which is more conducive to employee crea- tivity. Finally, AI enhances the accessibility and compre- hensibility of information with powerful data processing capabilities (Gibbard et al. 2025), helping employees to apply otherwise incomprehensible infor- mation to their work and improve their ability to innovate.

However, if HAI exceeds certain limits, it may lead to negative e ects such as information overload and tech- nical failures, which can cause stress for individuals. On the one hand, from a cognitive allocation perspective, employees need time to additionally understand the internal logic behind AI technology (Skaria, Satam, and Khalpey 2020), taking up mental resources that could have been used for innovation. Employees become accustomed to the solutions provided by AI 

BEHAVIOUR & INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 3

and thus lose the motivation to invest cognitive e ort in thinking on their own (Lindebaum, Vesa, and den Hond 2020), and without a deeper understanding and internalisation of these solutions, the brain processes the information superﬁcially, making it di cult to gen- erate innovative ideas. Second, Over-reliance on out- sourcing tasks to AI fosters mental rigidity and locks innovation pathways (Laursen and Salter 2006; Liao 2002), thereby hindering the stimulation of innovative ideas among team members. Finally, excessive AI invol- vement fosters a sense of technological displacement among employees (Wu and Hu 2018), potentially prompting them to adopt passive-aggressive strategies (such as resisting AI) and suppressing creative explora- tory behaviours. This leads to hypothesis H1: 

**H1**: There is an inverted U-shaped relationship between HAI and employee creativity.

## _2.2. The mediating role of cognitive outsourcing_

Given the scarcity of cognitive resources and the com- plexity of processing, employees tend to engage in cog- nitive outsourcing behaviours when AI can solve problems faster. The human cognitive system is charac- terised by an extended mindset, which o oads some internal activities to the environment to aid cognitive processing (Weis and Wiese 2022). ‘Knowing where information is’ rather than ‘remembering the infor- mation itself (Sparrow, Liu, and Wegner 2011).’ At low levels of HAI, employees do not yet have an in- depth understanding of the AI’s capabilities, resulting in a low level of cognitive outsourcing. However, as the interaction deepens, deeper trust in the AI prompts increased cognitive outsourcing. Because most AIs have powerful and versatile problem diagnosis and solving capabilities (Guha et al. 2023), employees perceive that they can accurately perform a variety of tasks with con- sistent and reliable results. Secondly, AIs provide employees with su cient information resources (Dwi- vedi et al. 2023) to help them process information and analyze data (Raisch and Krakowski 2021), and improve the e ciency of storing and transferring explicit knowl- edge (Pai et al. 2022). Addressing the problem of hand- ling large amounts of data, which are considered cumbersome and di cult to manage (Wu and Hu 2018).

However, when the degree of HAI is too high, AI may make employees resistant (Sverke et al. 2019), and cognitive outsourcing is reduced. A high degree of HAI may bring about a large amount of redundant information that exceeds the processing capacity of employees, creating information overload (Shao et al. 

4 M. CHEN ET AL.

2024). Meanwhile, from a psychological perspective, excessive HAI may cause employees to have a ‘self- e cacy crisis’ (Yan and Teng [2025)](#5465annals20170093-my-daily-tasks-relies-more-on-ai-zhang-q-x-h-wang-c-g-nerstad-h-ren-and-r-gao-co8-the-more-i-rely-on-ai-the-more-i-feel-that-my-ability-to-think-2022-motivational-climates-work-passion-and-independently-is-diminishing). Therefore, exces- sive HAI subjects employees to resource threats and losses, leading them to reduce trust in cognitive out- sourcing and proactively decrease outsourcing beha- viours. This leads to hypothesis H2: 

**H2**: HAI and cognitive outsourcing have an inverted U- shaped relationship.

Employees outsource routine tasks to AI and will instead reserve more energy for solving high-level pro- blems (Jia et al. 2024), utilising AI to reconﬁgure work - ows and innovation processes (Brougham and Haar [2018)](#employees-perform-ﬁnal-judgments-and-veriﬁcations-to-author-contributions-ensure-the-preservation-of-core-cognitive-capabilities-credit-minling-chen-funding-acquisition-methodology). At the same time, external storage reduces the burden on memory (Barr et al. [2015)](#employees-perform-ﬁnal-judgments-and-veriﬁcations-to-author-contributions-ensure-the-preservation-of-core-cognitive-capabilities-credit-minling-chen-funding-acquisition-methodology) and allows for easy mobilisation of materials needed for innovation when needed. In addition, the diverse information interactions brought about by cognitive outsourcing can help stimulate employee creativity. Through cogni- tive outsourcing to AI, employees are exposed to and assimilate new information, combine and utilise it to generate new ideas to solve work problems. By integrat- ing di erent pieces of information, employees can be motivated to ‘think outside the box’ to stimulate the generation of solutions to problems (Teodoridis, Bikard, and Vakili 2019). This leads to hypothesis H3: 

**H3**: Cognitive outsourcing mediates the inverted U- shaped relationship between HAI and employee creativity.

### _2.3. Moderating e_ _ects of team mastery motivational climate_

Team mastery motivational climate is a climate that emphasises supportive, collaborative, learning, and skill acquisition (Cerne et al. [2014)](#employees-perform-ﬁnal-judgments-and-veriﬁcations-to-author-contributions-ensure-the-preservation-of-core-cognitive-capabilities-credit-minling-chen-funding-acquisition-methodology), and signiﬁcantly acts on proactive innovation behaviours by in uencing the way employees manage their resources. Technol- ogies such as AI have brought about dramatic changes to employees’ work tasks, work processes, and division of labour (Einola and Khoreva 2023), and can organis- ational support employees in accessing resources? This may explain, in part, the alienation of innovation out- comes. Therefore, we introduce the variable of team mastery motivational climate to explore the moderating e ect on the relationship between HAI and cognitive outsourcing.

Speciﬁcally, in teams with a low team mastery moti- vational climate, employees are more concerned with task completion and individual performance, and mem- bers choose to maintain the status quo more for 

resource protection and acquisition. When HAI is mod- erate, members tend to rely on external technical sup- port to complete cognitive tasks, accelerating cognitive outsourcing; while in the over-interaction state, despite the risk of resource depletion such as technological dependence and cognitive overload, due to the lack of motivation to proactively optimise cognitive strategies, members intensify cognitive outsourcing behaviours due to the pressure of resource maintenance. However, in teams with a highly team mastery motivational cli- mate, members are more inclined to view HAI as a tool for capability expansion rather than a substitute for cognitive e ort, and this motivational orientation undermines cognitive outsourcing triggered by exces- sive interaction. First, teams require employees to initiate cognitive validation in AI use, such as question- ing algorithmic logic and supplementing contextualised knowledge, rather than directly adopting AI sugges- tions. This deep-processing behaviour forces employees to continuously activate their metacognitive abilities, respond more rationally to challenges during inter- actions, and avoid cognitive o oading due to techno- logical convenience (Skulmowski 2023). Secondly, by recognising employees’ value, the team mastery motiva- tional climate enhances employees’ innovative self- conﬁdence and sense of e cacy (Yin, Jiang, and Niu [2024)](#5465annals20170093-my-daily-tasks-relies-more-on-ai-zhang-q-x-h-wang-c-g-nerstad-h-ren-and-r-gao-co8-the-more-i-rely-on-ai-the-more-i-feel-that-my-ability-to-think-2022-motivational-climates-work-passion-and-independently-is-diminishing), which makes them believe more in their pro- blem-solving ability rather than relying on AI, and more able to experience autonomy and a sense of con- trol in their work tasks (Zhang et al. [2022)](#5465annals20170093-my-daily-tasks-relies-more-on-ai-zhang-q-x-h-wang-c-g-nerstad-h-ren-and-r-gao-co8-the-more-i-rely-on-ai-the-more-i-feel-that-my-ability-to-think-2022-motivational-climates-work-passion-and-independently-is-diminishing). This leads to hypothesis (Figure 1) H4: 

**H4**: The team mastery motivational climate moderates the inverted U-shaped e ect of HAI on cognitive out- sourcing, i.e. the inverted U-shaped curve between HAI and cognitive outsourcing is shifted to the left and tends to be atter for employees in a high team mastery motivational climate.

Based on the research focus of this paper, the dependency and cogni- tive autonomy dimensions were selected to test the extent of employees’ cognitive outsourcing during human-AI interaction. The scale consists of 11 question items, and a typical example is: ‘I believe external tools play a very important role in your cognitive processes.’ The Cronbach’s alpha for this scale is 0.920.

Team Mastery Motivational Climate (TMMC). Using the 6-item scale developed by Nerstad, Roberts, and Richardsen (2013), an example is: ‘My team encourages members to exchange ideas and opinions.’ The Cron- bach’s alpha for this scale was 0.883.

Employee Creativity (EC). Drawing on the 4-item employee self-assessed creativity scale developed by Baer and Oldham ([2006)](#employees-perform-ﬁnal-judgments-and-veriﬁcations-to-author-contributions-ensure-the-preservation-of-core-cognitive-capabilities-credit-minling-chen-funding-acquisition-methodology), a speciﬁc example is: ‘I fre- quently propose creative ideas that may improve organ- izational work conditions.’ The Cronbach’s alpha for this scale is 0.832.

Control variables: drawing on articles on HAI and AI use (Jia et al. 2024; Liu and Li 2025), gender, age, edu- cation background, and length of service were used as control variables.

A number of approaches were taken to minimise the impact of common methodological biases. First, in the design of the questionnaire, well-established and vali- dated scales were selected, and the questions were made as concise as possible and could be e ectively understood. Second, the questionnaire followed the code of ethics for social science research and was anon- ymous to minimise ethical issues and the creation of bias. Finally, all items were subjected to principal com- ponent analysis using Harman’s one-way test. Harman’s one-way test showed that after unrotated principal com- ponent analysis of all items for the four variables: human-AI interaction, cognitive outsourcing, employee creativity, and team mastery motivational climate, the ﬁrst factor obtained explained 36.45% of the variance, which is much lower than the baseline of 50%. In con- clusion, based on the above test results it indicates that there are not many CMB issues.

## _4.2. Reliability and validity_

As shown in [Table 2,](#42-reliability-and-validity) the Cronbach’s alpha for all vari- ables is greater than 0.8, which proves that the reliability of the questionnaire is high. Secondly, after testing the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) value and Bartlett’s spheri- city of the overall questionnaire, the results showed that the KMO value was 0.932 and the Bartlett’s test result passed the 0.000 signiﬁcance level. Subsequently, the structural validity of the scale was tested using conver- gent validity and discriminant validity. The results showed that the factor loadings \> 0.6, AVE \> 0.5, and CR \> 0.8, and all the indexes satisﬁed the critical values, indicating that the scale had good convergent validity. Second, this paper analyzes the inter-variable corre- lation matrix. The results show that the AVE square root values (values on the diagonal) of each variable in the matrix are greater than the values in the given rows and columns (see [Table 3)](#42-reliability-and-validity), which indicates that our scale has good discriminant validity.

Finally, a validation factor analysis (CFA) was per- formed using AMOS software. According to the results

## _4.3. Hypotheses testing_

Referring to the usual practice of curve studies, the inverted U-shaped e ect of human-AI interaction on employee creativity was examined by constructing squared terms, and the moderating e ect of team mas- tery motivational climate was examined by constructing interaction terms. Before constructing square terms and interaction terms, the variables were centred.

First, the inverted U-shaped e ect of human-AI interaction on employee creativity is tested. Model 4 is the e ect of control variables on employee creativity, and Model 5 adds HAI and HAI squared term based on Model 4, which shows that HAI has a signiﬁcant positive e ect on employee creativity (β = 0.252, _p_ \< 0.01), and HAI squared term has a signiﬁcant negative e ect on employee creativity (β = −0.191, _p_ \< 0.05). Fur- thermore, the standardised HAI values range from \[−2.51, 1.09\]. When x = −2.51, the curve’s slope k \> 0; when x = 1.09, the slope k \< 0. The value at the in ection point is -β1/2β2 = 0.66, which lies within the range of the independent variable. This indicates that HAI has an inverted U-shaped e ect on employee creativity pre- sents an inverted U-shaped e ect that ﬁrst rises and then falls, and H1 is conﬁrmed. Similarly, Model 1 is the e ect of control variables on cognitive outsourcing, and Model 5 adds HAI and HAI squared term based on Model 4, and the results show that HAI positively a ects cognitive outsourcing (β = 0.349, _p_ \< 0.01), and the HAI squared term negatively a ects cognitive outsourcing (β = −0.17, _p_ \< 0.05), which suggests that the e ect of HAI on cognitive outsourcing also shows a ﬁrst-rising and then falling inverted U-shaped e ect. H2 is conﬁrmed.

Second, the mediating e ect of cognitive outsourcing was tested. As shown in [Table 5](#other-resources-which-in-turn-facilitates-cognitive-out--51-theoretical-contributions-sourcing-however-excessive-interaction-may-trigger) Model 6, cognitive out- sourcing can positively a ect employee creativity (β = 0.359, _p_ \< 0.01). The data were further mediation tested using the MEDCURVE macro programme in SPSS with 5000 repetitive samples (at 95% conﬁdence level). The results are shown in [Table 6,](#is-a-key-resource-investment-strategy-adopted-by-52-management-enlightenment-employees-to-optimise-the-allocation-of-their-limited) taking low (mean-1SD), medium (mean), and high (mean+1SD) values for HAI, respectively, the mediation e ect of cognitive out- sourcing has been decreasing, and the conﬁdence inter- vals corresponding to the instantaneous mediation e ect do not contain 0 when HAI is taken at the low and medium levels, until HAI is taken at the high level, at which time the corresponding conﬁdence 

BEHAVIOUR & INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY 7

intervals contain 0. This suggests that cognitive outsour- cing plays a signiﬁcant mediating e ect in the nonlinear relationship between HAI and employee creativity, so H3 is conﬁrmed.

Finally, the moderating role of team mastery motiva- tional climate between HAI and cognitive outsourcing was tested. According to the results of Model 3 in [Table 5,](#other-resources-which-in-turn-facilitates-cognitive-out--51-theoretical-contributions-sourcing-however-excessive-interaction-may-trigger) the interaction term between the squared term of HAI and the interaction term of team mastery motivational climate has a signiﬁcantly negative e ect on cognitive outsourcing (β = −0.151, _p_ \< 0.01), which indicates that the team mastery motivational climate can modulate the inverted U-shaped relationship between HAI and cognitive outsourcing, and H4 is conﬁrmed. In order to more intuitively show the mod- erating e ect of team mastery motivational climate, this paper plotted the moderating e ect in [Figure 2.](#is-a-key-resource-investment-strategy-adopted-by-52-management-enlightenment-employees-to-optimise-the-allocation-of-their-limited) The enhancement e ect of HAI on cognitive outsourcing quickly reaches the threshold for employees in a high team mastery motivational climate. The turning point of the relationship between HAI and cognitive outsour- cing occurs later for employees in a low team mastery motivational climate, which suggests that the team mas- tery motivational climate plays a negative moderating role between the two.

# 5. Conclusion and discussion

Based on the COR theory, this study examined the non- linear impact mechanism of human-AI interaction on employee creativity. The main ﬁndings of the study are as follows:

First, this study conﬁrms the double-edged sword e ect of human-AI interaction: AI is a double-edged sword, and the principle of ‘moderation’ should be fol- lowed in order to maximise the potential of AI. Moder- ate interaction empowers employee creativity, while excessive interaction is a hindrance to creativity. There- fore, the results of human-AI interaction are not posi- tive, in part echoing the controversy (Karhade and Dong 2021; Yin, Jiang, and Niu [2024)](#5465annals20170093-my-daily-tasks-relies-more-on-ai-zhang-q-x-h-wang-c-g-nerstad-h-ren-and-r-gao-co8-the-more-i-rely-on-ai-the-more-i-feel-that-my-ability-to-think-2022-motivational-climates-work-passion-and-independently-is-diminishing) that over-reliance on AI hinders the development of employee creativity and corporate innovation. Moreover, this double- edged sword e ect may be more pronounced in knowl- edge-intensive industries closely tied to cognitive resources, whereas its intensity may diminish for stra- tegic decision-makers or labour-intensive positions. Second, cognitive outsourcing plays an important mediating role between human-AI interaction and employee creativity. According to the COR theory, in human-AI interaction scenarios, moderate interaction is seen as a way for individuals to gain access to infor- mation processing e ciency, technical support, and
